grammar.title: kindin · kindina
grammar.rule: Kindin kemur. Bjarni á kindina. Hann á hana.

tables.caption: hann · hún · það · þeir · þær · þau

grammar.note_en:
A noun names someone or something: kind “ewe”, hrútur “ram”. Its case is the form that shows its job in a sentence. The nominative (nf.) is the subject form, used for the person or thing doing something: Kindin kemur, “The ewe comes.” The accusative (þf.) is the object form used here for what someone owns, sees, finds, examines, takes or pulls: Bjarni á kindina, “Bjarni owns the ewe.” Kindin and kindina name the same ewe; the change shows her different job. English usually keeps the noun unchanged and relies on word order. Icelandic marks the difference on the noun as well. The verb still agrees with its subject, never its object.

The ending -ur often disappears in the masculine singular object: hrútur → hrút, “ram”. With the attached word for “the”, hrúturinn becomes hrútinn: Bjarni sér hrútinn, “Bjarni sees the ram.” In the feminine singular, kind “ewe” stays kind, but its definite form changes: kindin → kindina, “the ewe”. The neuter lamb “lamb” and lambið “the lamb” keep their forms. These patterns belong to these nouns; not every noun follows them. Bók becomes bókina when definite and an object: Bjarni tekur bókina, “Bjarni takes the book.” Names also change: Siggi → Sigga, Ketill → Ketil. Ásta sér Sigga og lambið means “Ásta sees Siggi and the lamb”. Siggi sér lambið og Ketil means “Siggi sees the lamb and Ketill”.

An adjective describes a noun and agrees with it in gender, number and case. Compare grá kind “a grey ewe” and Siggi sér gráa kind, “Siggi sees a grey ewe”; lítill hrútur “a little ram” and Siggi sér lítinn hrút, “Siggi sees a little ram”. In the plural, litlir hrútar becomes litla hrúta: Jón finnur … litla hrúta, “Jón finds … little rams”. Feminine plural gráar kindur stays the same: Jón finnur gráar kindur, “Jón finds grey ewes”. The changed forms in the table are object forms, not new words for different animals. These are adjectives before indefinite nouns, with no “the”. Learn these examples together; adjective endings have several patterns.

A pronoun stands in for a noun. The object pronouns here are hann (masculine singular), hana (feminine singular), það (neuter singular), þá (masculine plural), þær (feminine plural), þau (neuter plural or a mixed group). Grammatical gender matters even for animals and things: Bjarni … á hana, “Bjarni owns it”, refers to kind, feminine; Bjarni … dregur hann í dilkinn, “Bjarni pulls it into the pen”, refers to hrútur, masculine. Jón finnur kindur og skoðar þær means “Jón finds ewes and examines them”. Óli sér hrúta; hann dregur þá í dilkinn means “Óli sees rams; he pulls them into the pen”. Ketill sér lömb og skoðar þau means “Ketill sees lambs and examines them”. In Bjarni takes the book, Siggi sees him and afi sees it, the Icelandic distinguishes hann “him” (Bjarni) from hana “it” (bókin, feminine). The object form hann happens to be identical to the subject form hann. Hún changes to hana, and þeir changes to þá.

Hver? asks “who?” as subject: Hver á lambið?, “Who owns the lamb?” Hvern? asks about a masculine singular object: Hvern á Bjarni? Hrútinn eða hundinn?, “Which one does Bjarni own? The ram or the dog?” Hvað? means “what?”: Hvað á Jón?, “What does Jón own?” These questions concern ownership, so á means “owns”, not the place word á “on”. Eiga is the dictionary form: Bjarni á, “Bjarni owns”; the plural eiga is learned with the other verbs later. Do not confuse the object with the owner.

Um takes an accusative object too. Here it names a time: um kvöldið, “in the evening”; um haustið, “in autumn”. Both are neuter forms whose accusative looks like their nominative. This is a property of neuter nouns, not an exception to the case requirement. Í dilkinn, “into the pen”, remains a whole direction phrase for now. It describes movement into a place, unlike earlier phrases that tell where something is. Do not use its ending as a general rule for every place phrase yet. Báðir strákarnir, “both boys”, is a subject phrase in this chapter; its other cases come later. New verb forms such as tekur “takes”, finnur “finds”, dregur “pulls” and vill “wants” are supported reading forms, not conjugation exercises. All the scenes and questions remain in the present tense.

words_with_history.note_en: A mark is a sign; here it is an earmark cut into a sheep’s ear to identify its owner. Farms’ marks were recorded in a markaskrá, an earmark register. The boys can bring the stray home, but they cannot identify its owner from its unfamiliar mark.
